title: Build a Company Research Agent with Search, Scraping, and Data Enrichment
summary: Build a company research agent with evidence-linked search, page retrieval, selective enrichment, clear budgets, and a reviewable supplier brief.
body_markdown:
A useful company research agent produces an evidence-backed brief that someone can act on. It identifies the right business, reads the pages that matter, fills specific gaps, and separates verified facts from estimates. Giving it more tools helps only when those tools improve that result.


This reference workflow combines web search, page retrieval, and optional company enrichment. It is designed around a shared tool layer such as o11, so the application can discover and authorize capabilities through one integration. It is an implementation recipe, not a report of a live paid run. Availability, account requirements, and prices must be checked for the exact operations you select.


## Define the brief before the search


Start with the decision the reader needs to make. A sales researcher wants buying context. An investor wants a business description and evidence of traction. A developer evaluating a supplier wants API fit, documentation, and operational constraints. One generic company summary satisfies none of these well.


For a supplier evaluation, define six fields: legal or trading name, canonical website, product description, intended customer, relevant technical capabilities, and unresolved questions. Attach a source reference and observation date to every factual field. A missing field should remain missing, with a reason such as “not stated in the reviewed documentation.”


Set the stopping condition at the same time. For example, stop after finding the official product page, official documentation, current pricing page, and one independent source, or after eight retrievals. Eight is an illustrative workflow limit, not a claim that eight pages always establish the truth. A bounded assignment is easier to evaluate than “research this company thoroughly.”


## Separate discovery, reading, and enrichment


Search answers where to look. Retrieval answers what a selected page says. Enrichment answers a defined question about a matched entity. These are separate jobs and should have separate acceptance criteria.


[Exa’s search reference](https://exa.ai/docs/reference/search) documents web discovery with optional page contents.[Firecrawl’s scrape guide](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/scrape) documents extracting content from a known URL. Those capabilities can occupy different stages even when one supplier offers both.


An effective first pass searches the company name together with its domain, then follows official navigation to product, documentation, and pricing pages. Preserve the final redirected domain. If two companies share a name, location and product clues become disambiguation evidence. Do not merge their records because the search engine put them next to each other.


Only enrich after resolving identity.[People Data Labs describes company enrichment as a one-to-one company match](https://docs.peopledatalabs.com/docs/company-enrichment-api) . In this design, enrichment fills requested gaps; it does not overwrite contradictory first-party evidence without review.


## Use a claim ledger instead of a pile of pages


Store observations as small claims with their supporting material. A practical record contains a claim identifier, field name, proposed value, source URL, page title, relevant passage, retrieval time, and status. Status might be supported, conflicting, inferred, or unresolved.


Consider the statement “the supplier supports asynchronous video generation.” The ledger should point to the documentation section describing submission and completion. A marketing phrase such as “create videos instantly” does not establish an asynchronous API contract. The distinction matters when an engineer later estimates implementation work.


Keep short source excerpts internally for verification, subject to source terms and retention policy. The final brief should paraphrase and link rather than reproduce entire pages. Also store the retrieval outcome. A blocked documentation page means evidence is unavailable, not that the feature is absent.


This structure supports revisions. When a source changes, you know which claims need another look. It also makes a useful user interface possible: a reader can open the evidence behind a field instead of trusting a paragraph generated from an opaque context window.


## Route tools by the missing information


The agent should request a capability because of a gap in the brief. If the company domain is unknown, search. If the pricing URL is known but unread, retrieve it. If a public company identifier is required, use the relevant registry or structured company service. If the answer is already in a reviewed page, reuse that evidence within the permitted freshness window.


Build a routing table before letting the model choose freely:


Missing information First action Escalation


Canonical company website Search and inspect candidates Ask the user to resolve ambiguity


Product capabilities Read official documentation Search exact feature terminology


Pricing model Read current pricing and billing docs Mark unknown or request a quote


Company attributes Read official company material Use an authorized enrichment source


Conflicting claims Compare dates and definitions Preserve the conflict for review


The shared layer handles access and execution; the research application still owns this decision policy.[Our tool selection guide](https://o11.ai/blog/choose-agent-tool-set) explains how to keep that policy small enough to inspect.


## Budget the investigation, including uncertainty


Plan calls before starting expensive branches. An illustrative assignment might allow two searches, six page retrievals, and one enrichment lookup. If assumed costs are $0.02 per search, $0.01 per retrieval, and $0.08 per enrichment, tool usage totals $0.18: $0.04 + $0.06 + $0.08. These are invented planning inputs, not supplier quotes. Model inference, storage, and retries are additional.


The important unit is cost per accepted brief. If ten attempted briefs cost $1.80 and only six meet the evidence standard, the observed tool cost per accepted brief would be $0.30. Do not divide by ten and hide the failed work. No such experiment was performed for this article; the calculation illustrates the denominator you should record.


For o11, inspect the operation and selected account mode before execution. A customer-account call and a wallet-funded call have different billing paths. A catalog entry alone does not establish live execution or wallet-funded availability. Use[the workflow cost model](https://o11.ai/blog/multi-tool-agent-cost-estimation) to include all of these branches.


## Keep research inputs out of the control plane


Company websites are research material. They cannot expand the agent’s permissions, change the assignment, or instruct it to reveal credentials. Treat page text as untrusted data even when the page belongs to a legitimate company. A compromised page or user-generated section can contain instructions that have nothing to do with the research task.


Use read-only tool scopes for this workflow. The brief does not need email sending, CRM mutation, purchases outside its authorized tools, or deployment permissions. Keep supplier credentials in the execution service rather than the model context. The model needs operation descriptions and safe results, not raw secrets.


Minimize enrichment fields. If the task concerns company software capabilities, personal phone numbers add cost and exposure without improving the answer. Decide what to retain and when to delete it. These choices should follow the actual purpose of the research, rather than everything a provider happens to return.


## Handle partial results without inventing a complete story


Failures should remain local to the affected field or company. If pricing retrieval fails, finish the product and technical sections and mark pricing unresolved. If enrichment returns an ambiguous match, keep the verified domain and omit the uncertain attributes. A batch of twenty companies should not lose nineteen good briefs because one company has an inaccessible site.


Distinguish an empty result from a failed request. An empty successful search may justify a broader query. A timeout needs a bounded retry or a later attempt. An unknown paid invocation needs status or reconciliation before another purchase. Reusing a different request key because a response was lost can create duplicate costs.


The output should expose the remaining work: “Pricing page could not be retrieved; verify before budgeting,” for example. That sentence is more useful than a confident price inferred from an old article.[Source-checking research](https://o11.ai/blog/source-checking-research-agent) covers field-level evidence review in more detail.


## Review the result as a decision document


Before accepting a brief, ask whether a reader can distinguish facts, interpretation, and unanswered questions. Check identity first, then sources, then the conclusion. A beautifully written summary about the wrong company fails before style becomes relevant.


For a small evaluation set, choose varied cases: a company with clear docs, one with multiple brands, one with sparse public information, and one with recently changed pricing. Establish expected facts manually. Evaluate factual support, useful coverage, explicit uncertainty, run cost, and time to an accepted brief. Do not optimize for the number of fields filled if the agent is rewarded for guessing.


The next implementation step is a single-company workflow with a claim ledger and a hard retrieval budget. Expand to batches only after the brief is consistently useful. The productivity benefit comes from turning tool access into a repeatable research process that keeps its evidence intact.


## Example: reviewing a supplier brief


Imagine a fictional developer evaluating a document-processing supplier. The agent finds an official product page saying it handles invoices and documentation describing asynchronous extraction. It also finds a third-party profile with an employee estimate. The brief should treat those as three different observations, with separate evidence and confidence.


The useful conclusion might be: the supplier appears technically relevant because its documented workflow accepts invoice files and exposes job completion. Commercial fit remains unresolved because the reviewed pages do not establish the applicable account price. The employee estimate is background context, not evidence of API reliability.


A reviewer can now make a targeted next decision: inspect a representative output and obtain the relevant commercial terms. The agent does not need ten more generic company pages. It needs evidence about two remaining questions.


This example also suggests an acceptance check. Remove the product-page source from the record and ask whether the conclusion still has support. Change the company domain and confirm that identity review catches the mismatch. Replace a current pricing page with an old announcement and check whether the date qualification remains visible. These are proposed evaluation cases, not tests reported as executed here.
